tool.name: Vendor Compliance Questionnaire
tool.description:
Generate compliance questionnaires for organizations evaluating third-party 
products to integrate with the EUDIW ecosystem. Select your organisation's 
role, the product category you're evaluating, and the regulatory sources 
to include.

**Scope**: VCQ targets private sector commercial products. Public-sector-only 
mandates and organization-only requirements (registration with authorities, 
HR/personnel, financial obligations) are covered in the RCA tool.

requirements.requirement: Intermediaries shall not store data about the content of transactions
requirements.explanation:
The no-storage mandate is the central privacy protection for wallet users
when interacting through intermediaries. Article 5b(10) establishes an
absolute prohibition: vendors acting on behalf of RPs are deemed to be
relying parties themselves and shall not store data about the content of
the transaction. There are no exceptions — this is not a "minimize" or
"limit" obligation but a full prohibition on storage.

The ARF reinforces this through multiple HLRs:
- AS-RP-51-011: the intermediary must forward user attributes to the
  intermediated RP without processing or storing them
- AS-RP-51-013: the intermediary must delete any PIDs or attestations obtained
  from the Wallet Unit completely and immediately after forwarding
- AS-RP-51-012: the intermediary must not combine data from multiple
  transactions or across different intermediated RPs

The product must demonstrate architectural controls that enforce this
mandate — for example, in-memory-only processing, no persistence layer
for transaction content, and no logging of attribute values. Transient
processing in memory for the duration of a single request-response cycle
is permissible, but no data may survive beyond forwarding completion.
requirements.legalText:
Intermediaries acting on behalf of relying parties shall be deemed to be
relying parties and shall not store data about the content of the transaction.

requirements.requirement: Implement a Data Processing Agreement meeting GDPR Article 28 requirements
requirements.explanation:
When intermediaries process personal data on behalf of the RP, they act
as data processors under GDPR. Article 28(3) mandates a binding written
contract (DPA) between the controller (RP) and processor (intermediary)
that governs the processing relationship.

The DPA must address all eight mandatory provisions of Article 28(3):
- (a) Processing only on documented instructions from the controller,
  including rules on international data transfers
- (b) Confidentiality obligations for all authorized personnel
- (c) Implementation of Article 32 security measures
- (d) Conditions for engaging sub-processors (see VEND-CORE-013)
- (e) Assistance with data subject rights requests (see VEND-CORE-010)
- (f) Assistance with security, breach notification, and DPIA
  obligations (Articles 32-36)
- (g) Deletion or return of data at contract end (see VEND-CORE-014)
- (h) Audit rights and compliance demonstration (see VEND-CORE-003)

In the EUDI Wallet context, the DPA must also specifically address the
no-storage mandate (Article 5b(10) eIDAS) and the forward-only nature
of intermediary data handling, since these constraints are unique to
wallet intermediation and go beyond standard GDPR processor obligations.

The DPA must be in writing (including electronic form) per Article 28(9).
requirements.legalText:
Processing by a processor shall be governed by a contract or other legal act
under Union or Member State law, that is binding on the processor with regard
to the controller and that sets out the subject-matter and duration of the
processing, the nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal
data and categories of data subjects and the obligations and rights of the
controller. That contract or other legal act shall stipulate, in particular,
that the processor: (a) processes the personal data only on documented
instructions from the controller; (b) ensures that persons authorised to
process the personal data have committed themselves to confidentiality;
(c) takes all measures required pursuant to Article 32; [...]
(h) makes available to the controller all information necessary to
demonstrate compliance with the obligations laid down in this Article and
allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, conducted by the
controller or another auditor mandated by the controller.

requirements.requirement: Provide audit rights to the Relying Party
requirements.explanation:
Article 28(3)(h) imposes two distinct obligations on the processor
(intermediary vendor):

1. **Information provision**: the processor must make available to the
   controller (RP) all information necessary to demonstrate compliance
   with the processing obligations set out in Article 28
2. **Active audit support**: the processor must allow for and actively
   contribute to audits, including on-site inspections, conducted by
   the controller or by an independent auditor mandated by the controller

In the EUDI Wallet intermediary context, audits are particularly
important for verifying:
- Compliance with the no-storage mandate (Art 5b(10) eIDAS) — that no
  transaction content is persisted beyond the forwarding operation
- Correct implementation of the forward-only architecture (AS-RP-51-011)
- Security of cryptographic key management for access certificates
- Proper handling of sub-processor relationships
- Data isolation between intermediated RPs (no cross-RP correlation)

The last sentence of Article 28(3) also obliges the processor to
immediately inform the controller if an instruction infringes GDPR or
other EU/Member State data protection law — this is an active
compliance monitoring obligation, not just a passive audit right.

Vendors should be prepared to demonstrate compliance through a
combination of third-party certifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II),
architectural documentation, and facilitation of direct inspections.
requirements.legalText:
The processor shall make available to the controller all information 
necessary to demonstrate compliance with the obligations laid down in 
this Article and allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, 
conducted by the controller or another auditor mandated by the controller.

requirements.requirement: Register as a Relying Party indicating intermediary status
requirements.explanation:
Any entity acting as an intermediary must register as a Relying Party
with Member State authorities before interacting with EUDI Wallets.
The registration is governed by two layers of requirements:

**Legal framework (eIDAS + IR 2025/848):**
- Article 5b(1) eIDAS: base obligation to register in the Member State
  where the RP is established
- IR 2025/848, Article 3: Member States must set up human-readable and
  machine-readable (API) interfaces for registration
- IR 2025/848, Annex I: specifies the 17 data elements to be provided,
  including point 14 ("indication of reliance on an intermediary") and
  point 15 ("relationship to intermediated RPs")
- IR 2025/848, Article 5: registration policies and verification

**ARF requirements:**
- AS-RP-51-001 (Topic 52): an intermediary must register as a Relying Party,
  indicating that it will act as an intermediary
- Topic 27: general RP registration including intended uses and
  requested attribute sets

Upon successful registration, the intermediary receives:
- An access certificate (via Article 7, IR 2025/848) containing the
  intermediary's own name and unique identifier
- Optionally, registration certificates for each intended use (via
  Article 8, IR 2025/848)

The product should support the full registration lifecycle via the
TS5 REST API (see VEND-CORE-045) or provide a management interface
for manual registration workflows.
requirements.legalText:
Where a relying party intends to rely upon European Digital Identity
Wallets for the provision of public or private services by means of
digital interaction, the relying party shall register in the Member
State where it is established.

requirements.requirement: Maintain a valid Relying Party Access Certificate
requirements.explanation:
Access certificates are the primary trust mechanism between wallet units
and relying parties. The RP connector must obtain and maintain a valid
wallet-relying party access certificate to authenticate itself to
wallet units during every presentation transaction.

**Certificate issuance and policy (IR 2025/848):**
- Article 7(1): Member States must authorise at least one certificate
  authority to issue wallet-relying party access certificates
- Article 7(2): access certificates are issued exclusively to
  registered wallet-relying parties
- Annex IV: the certificate must comply with ETSI EN 319411-1 NCP
  requirements and the harmonised certificate policy
- The certificate contains the RP's (or intermediary's) name and
  unique identifier — this is how wallet units identify the requester

**Usage requirements (ARF):**
- AS-WP-06-004 (Topic 6): the RP connector and wallet unit must perform
  Relying Party authentication in all PID or attestation presentation
  transactions, whether proximity or remote, using the access certificate
- AS-RP-06-001 (emptied in ARF v2.8.0, concept covered by AS-WP-06-004/AS-RP-06-004):
  the access certificate must be included in the presentation
  request by value, not by reference, ensuring atomic self-contained
  transactions
- AS-RP-51-006 (Topic 52): when acting on behalf of an intermediated RP,
  the intermediary includes its own access certificate alongside the
  RP's registration certificate and EW-DM-44-018 extension data

The product must implement certificate lifecycle management including
monitoring for expiration, automated or assisted renewal, secure
private key storage (preferably HSM-backed), and emergency revocation
and replacement procedures.
requirements.legalText:
Member States shall authorise at least one certificate authority to issue
wallet-relying party access certificates. Member States shall ensure that
providers of wallet-relying party access certificates issue wallet-relying
party access certificates exclusively to registered wallet-relying parties.

requirements.requirement: Implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures
requirements.explanation:
Article 32(1) GDPR mandates that both controllers and processors
implement technical and organisational security measures appropriate to
the risk, taking into account the state of the art, implementation
costs, and the nature/scope/context of processing.

Article 32(1) specifically enumerates four categories of measures:
- (a) Pseudonymization and encryption of personal data
- (b) Ability to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity,
  availability, and resilience of processing systems
- (c) Ability to restore availability and access to data in a timely
  manner after a physical or technical incident
- (d) Regular testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of
  measures (penetration testing, vulnerability scanning, red-teaming)

In the EUDI Wallet intermediary context, the following security
considerations are particularly critical:
- Secure handling of cryptographic material (access certificate private
  keys, signing keys) — preferably in HSMs or equivalent
- Transport-layer security (TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites) for
  all wallet-to-intermediary and intermediary-to-RP communication
- Application-layer encryption for sensitive payloads where applicable
- Network segmentation and access controls between RP tenants
- Secure development lifecycle (SDLC) practices for the product
- Incident detection capabilities (SIEM, anomaly detection, IDS/IPS)

The vendor should demonstrate appropriateness through certifications
(ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, CSA STAR) and documented risk assessments
per Article 32(2) that specifically address the wallet intermediation
processing context.
requirements.legalText:
Taking into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation 
and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as 
the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms 
of natural persons, the controller and processor shall implement appropriate 
technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security 
appropriate to the risk.

requirements.requirement: Notify the RP of data breaches without undue delay
requirements.explanation:
Article 33(2) GDPR requires the processor (intermediary) to notify the
controller (RP) without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal
data breach. This obligation is time-critical because it sits at the
start of a cascading notification chain:

**The breach notification chain:**
1. Processor → Controller: "without undue delay" (Art 33(2))
2. Controller → Supervisory Authority: within 72 hours of becoming
   aware (Art 33(1)), unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk
3. Controller → Data Subjects: "without undue delay" if the breach is
   likely to result in a high risk to rights and freedoms (Art 34(1))

The processor's notification must provide sufficient information for
the controller to fulfil its own obligations under Article 33(3):
- (a) Nature of the breach, including categories and approximate
  number of data subjects and records concerned
- (b) Name and contact details of the DPO or other contact point
- (c) Description of likely consequences of the breach
- (d) Description of measures taken or proposed to address the breach
  and mitigate its adverse effects

In the EUDI Wallet intermediary context, breaches may involve:
- Compromise of access certificate private keys
- Unauthorized access to transaction metadata or logs
- Failure of the no-storage controls (accidental data persistence)
- Interception of wallet presentations during forwarding

The vendor should have a documented incident response plan with
defined escalation paths, 24/7 security operations capability, and
contractually committed notification timeframes (ideally within hours,
not days) to ensure the RP can meet its 72-hour supervisory authority
notification deadline.
requirements.legalText:
The processor shall notify the controller without undue delay after
becoming aware of a personal data breach.

requirements.requirement: Ensure personnel authorized to process data are bound by confidentiality
requirements.explanation:
Article 28(3)(b) GDPR requires the processor to ensure that all persons
authorised to process personal data have committed themselves to
confidentiality or are under an appropriate statutory obligation of
confidentiality. This is a prerequisite obligation — it must be in place
*before* personnel are granted access to personal data.

**Scope of the obligation:**
- All employees with access to wallet transaction data, system logs,
  configuration data, or cryptographic material
- Contractors, temporary staff, and consultants
- Sub-processor personnel (flow-down via Art 28(4))
- On-call and support staff who may access production systems

In the EUDI Wallet intermediary context, confidentiality is particularly
critical because personnel may have transient access to:
- PID attributes (name, date of birth, nationality) during forwarding
- Attestation content during verification operations
- Access certificate private keys and signing material
- Transaction metadata that could reveal user behaviour patterns

The product vendor should demonstrate:
- Contractual confidentiality clauses in all employment/service agreements
- Background checks and security vetting proportionate to access level
- Role-based access control (RBAC) enforcing least-privilege
- Regular security awareness training including wallet-specific scenarios
- Immediate access revocation upon role change or contract termination
requirements.legalText:
The processor shall ensure that persons authorised to process the 
personal data have committed themselves to confidentiality or are 
under an appropriate statutory obligation of confidentiality.

requirements.requirement: Process personal data only on documented instructions from the RP
requirements.explanation:
Article 28(3)(a) GDPR imposes a fundamental limitation on the processor:
personal data may only be processed on documented instructions from the
controller (RP). This is the cornerstone of the controller-processor
relationship — the processor has no autonomous decision-making authority
over the purposes or means of processing.

**The instruction-only principle has two important qualifications:**
1. International transfers: the instruction scope explicitly includes
   rules on transfers to third countries or international organisations.
   The processor must not transfer data outside the EEA unless the
   controller's documented instructions permit it and appropriate
   safeguards (Art 46) or derogations (Art 49) are in place.
2. Legal override: if Union or Member State law requires the processor
   to process data beyond the controller's instructions, the processor
   must inform the controller of that legal requirement *before*
   processing, unless the law prohibits such disclosure on important
   grounds of public interest (see VEND-CORE-012).

In the EUDI Wallet intermediary context, this principle is reinforced
by the eIDAS Article 5b(10) no-storage mandate (VEND-CORE-001) and the
ARF forward-only architecture (AS-RP-51-011). The intermediary must:
- Process wallet data exclusively for the purpose of forwarding to
  the intermediated RP — no analytics, profiling, or product improvement
- Not repurpose transaction metadata for any secondary use
- Maintain a documented record of the RP's processing instructions
- Implement technical controls that prevent processing outside scope
requirements.legalText:
The processor shall process the personal data only on documented 
instructions from the controller, including with regard to transfers 
of personal data to a third country or an international organisation,
unless required to do so by Union or Member State law to which the
processor is subject; in such a case, the processor shall inform the
controller of that legal requirement before processing, unless that
law prohibits such information on important grounds of public interest.

requirements.requirement: Support data subject rights requests
requirements.explanation:
Article 28(3)(e) GDPR requires the processor to assist the controller
by appropriate technical and organisational measures, insofar as
possible, for the fulfilment of the controller's obligation to respond
to data subject rights requests under GDPR Chapter III.

**Data subject rights that may be exercised (Chapter III):**
- Art 15: Right of access — confirmation of processing and copy of data
- Art 16: Right to rectification — correction of inaccurate data
- Art 17: Right to erasure ("right to be forgotten") — deletion
- Art 18: Right to restriction of processing
- Art 20: Right to data portability — structured, machine-readable format
- Art 21: Right to object to processing
- Art 22: Rights related to automated decision-making and profiling

In the EUDI Wallet intermediary context, the no-storage mandate
(Art 5b(10) eIDAS, VEND-CORE-001) fundamentally limits the scope of
data subject requests since the intermediary should not hold any
transaction content data. However, the intermediary may still process:
- Configuration and registration data (RP identifiers, intended uses)
- Audit logs and transaction metadata (timestamps, success/failure)
- Certificate-related data (access certificate details)

The vendor must provide:
- Technical capability to search and identify all data relating to a
  specific data subject across all systems (including backups and logs)
- Documented procedures for handling each type of DSAR
- Committed response timeframes to assist the controller in meeting
  the one-month response deadline (Art 12(3))
- Audit trail of DSAR handling for compliance verification
requirements.legalText:
The processor shall, taking into account the nature of the processing,
assist the controller by appropriate technical and organisational 
measures, insofar as this is possible, for the fulfilment of the 
controller's obligation to respond to requests for exercising the 
data subject's rights laid down in Chapter III.

requirements.requirement: Display both intermediary and RP identity to wallet users
requirements.explanation:
Article 5b(8) eIDAS requires relying parties to identify themselves
to the user when relying on EUDI Wallets. For intermediaries, this
creates a dual-identity disclosure obligation: the wallet user must
see both the intermediary's identity and the identity of the
intermediated RP on whose behalf the request is made.

**The mechanism for dual-identity display (ARF Topic 52):**
- AS-RP-51-005: the intermediated RP specifies its identity data (name,
  unique identifier, Registrar URL, intended use identifier and
  description) when requesting a presentation through the intermediary
- AS-RP-51-006: the intermediary includes in each presentation request:
  (a) its own access certificate (containing its name and identifier),
  (b) the RP's registration certificate (if available, per AS-RP-51-003),
  and (c) the EW-DM-44-018 extension data for the intermediated RP
- AS-RP-51-008: the wallet unit displays the names and identifiers of both
  the intermediary and the intermediated RP when asking for user
  approval, as described in AS-WP-06-009

**EW-DM-44-018 extension fields (included per-request):**
- (a) User-friendly name of the Relying Party
- (b) Unique identifier of the Relying Party
- (c) User-friendly description of the intended use
- (d) URL of the Registrar of the Relying Party
- (e) Identifier of the intended use

This dual-identity mechanism enables informed consent — the user can
see who is technically requesting their data (intermediary) and who
will ultimately receive and use it (intermediated RP). The wallet unit
can also optionally verify the registered information with the Registrar
(AS-RP-51-009) to confirm that the intermediary-RP relationship is genuine.
requirements.legalText:
Where relying parties intend to rely upon European Digital Identity 
Wallets, they shall identify themselves to the user.

requirements.requirement: Inform the RP of any legal requirement to process data beyond instructions
requirements.explanation:
The second part of Article 28(3)(a) GDPR addresses the scenario where
the processor is required by Union or Member State law to process
personal data beyond the controller's documented instructions — for
example, in response to a court order, law enforcement data access
request, or regulatory investigation.

**The dual obligation:**
1. The processor must inform the controller of the legal requirement
   *before* processing the data beyond instructions
2. Exception: the processor is not required to inform the controller
   if the law prohibits such disclosure on important grounds of public
   interest (e.g., secrecy orders accompanying criminal investigations)

In the EUDI Wallet intermediary context, this obligation intersects
with the no-storage mandate (Art 5b(10) eIDAS). Since the intermediary
should not hold transaction content data, the scope of data that could
be subject to legal demands is limited to:
- Transaction metadata and audit logs
- Registration and configuration data
- Cryptographic material (access certificate data)
- Server-side operational logs

The vendor should have:
- A documented process for evaluating and responding to government
  access requests, including legal review procedures
- A commitment to challenge overbroad or unlawful requests
- A transparency report or willingness to disclose statistics on
  government access requests received and complied with
- Clear documentation of all jurisdictions where it is subject to
  data access laws (including foreign surveillance laws)
requirements.legalText:
Unless required to do so by Union or Member State law to which the
processor is subject; in such a case, the processor shall inform the
controller of that legal requirement before processing, unless that
law prohibits such information on important grounds of public interest.

requirements.requirement: Obtain RP authorization before engaging sub-processors
requirements.explanation:
Article 28(2) GDPR prohibits the processor from engaging another
processor (sub-processor) without the prior written authorisation of
the controller. This is a fundamental control that ensures the RP
retains oversight of the entire processing chain.

**Two authorisation models are available:**
1. **Specific authorisation**: the RP approves each sub-processor
   individually before engagement. This gives maximum control.
2. **General authorisation**: the RP grants blanket permission, but
   the processor must inform the RP of any intended changes
   (additions or replacements of sub-processors), thereby giving
   the RP the opportunity to object to such changes.

**Flow-down obligations (Article 28(4)):**
When engaging a sub-processor, the same data protection obligations
from the controller-processor contract must be imposed on the
sub-processor via a binding contract. Critically:
- The initial processor remains **fully liable** for the sub-processor's
  performance — this cannot be contracted away
- The sub-processor must be bound by equivalent security measures,
  confidentiality, no-storage mandate compliance, and audit rights

In the EUDI Wallet intermediary context, sub-processors may include:
- Cloud infrastructure providers (IaaS/PaaS)
- HSM-as-a-Service providers for key management
- Certificate management service providers
- Monitoring and logging service providers
- CDN or DDoS mitigation providers handling encrypted traffic

The DPA (VEND-CORE-002) must specify whether the authorisation model
is specific or general, and the advance notice period for changes.
requirements.legalText:
The processor shall not engage another processor without prior specific 
or general written authorisation of the controller. In the case of 
general written authorisation, the processor shall inform the controller 
of any intended changes concerning the addition or replacement of other 
processors, thereby giving the controller the opportunity to object to
such changes.

requirements.requirement: Delete or return personal data at end of contract
requirements.explanation:
Article 28(3)(g) GDPR gives the controller (RP) the choice: at the
end of the service contract, the processor must either delete or
return all personal data, and must also delete existing copies —
unless Union or Member State law requires continued storage.

**Key aspects of the obligation:**
- The choice (delete vs return) belongs to the controller, not the
  processor — the DPA should clearly specify which option applies
- "All personal data" includes data in primary systems, backups,
  disaster recovery sites, logs, and any derived data
- The processor must certify completion of deletion
- The retention exception for legal requirements must be documented
  and the specific legal basis identified

**Intersection with the eIDAS no-storage mandate:**
In the EUDI Wallet intermediary context, the no-storage mandate
(Art 5b(10), VEND-CORE-001) means the intermediary should already
hold minimal personal data at any point. At contract termination,
the data that may need deletion or return includes:
- Registration and configuration data (RP identifiers, intended uses)
- Audit logs containing transaction metadata
- Certificate and key management records
- Any DPA-related documentation containing personal data references
- Data in backups that may contain historical transaction metadata

The vendor should provide:
- A documented data return/deletion procedure with defined timelines
- A deletion certificate or formal attestation upon completion
- A commitment to delete data from all backup media within a
  specified timeframe (which may be longer than primary deletion)
- Identification of any data subject to legal retention requirements
requirements.legalText:
At the choice of the controller, the processor shall delete or return 
all the personal data to the controller after the end of the provision 
of services relating to processing, and delete existing copies unless
Union or Member State law requires storage of the personal data.

requirements.requirement: Register each intermediated RP at the appropriate Registrar
requirements.explanation:
ARF HLR AS-RP-51-003 mandates that an intermediary SHALL register each
intermediated Relying Party at a Registrar in the Member State where
that intermediated RP is established. This is a per-RP, per-Member-State
obligation — a multi-market intermediary must interface with multiple
national Registrars.

**The registration obligation has two elements:**
1. **Registration at the Registrar**: the intermediary registers the
   intermediated RP according to the requirements in Topic 44
   (registration certificates for RPs), providing the Annex I data
   set including the intermediary-specific fields (pts 14-15)
2. **Registration certificate acquisition**: if the Registrar's
   associated certificate authority issues registration certificates
   (per IR 2025/848 Art 8 — this is optional per Member State), the
   intermediary SHALL receive a registration certificate for each
   registered intended use of the intermediated RP

**Annex I intermediary-specific data fields:**
- Point 14: indication that the RP relies upon an intermediary
- Point 15: association to the specific intermediary acting on behalf
  of the RP

The implementing regulation (IR 2025/848) specifies in Article 5:
- Art 5(1): the information set out in Annex I must be provided
- Art 5(2): information must be accurate at time of registration
- Art 5(3): updates must be provided without undue delay

This registration is a prerequisite for the dual-identity display
mechanism (VEND-CORE-011, AS-RP-51-006) and the wallet-side Registrar
verification (AS-RP-51-009). Without proper registration, presentation
requests will lack the registration certificate and the Registrar
will not be able to confirm the intermediary-RP relationship.
requirements.legalText:
Wallet-relying parties shall at least provide the information set out 
in Annex I to national registers. Annex I(14-15) requires indication 
of intermediary status and association to intermediated RPs.

requirements.requirement: Provide legal evidence of RP relationship when registering
requirements.explanation:
ARF HLR AS-RP-51-004 requires the intermediary to provide legally valid
evidence that the intermediated RP will indeed use the intermediary's
services to interact with wallet units. This creates a two-party
verification chain:

**Step 1 — Intermediary provides evidence:**
The intermediary submits legally valid documentation to the Registrar.
The ARF notes suggest a contract between the intermediary and the
intermediated RP as a typical form of evidence, but other forms may
include power of attorney, letter of authorisation, or equivalent
legal instruments per Member State law.

**Step 2 — Registrar verifies evidence:**
The Registrar SHALL verify this evidence and, if found correct, SHALL
register the relationship between the intermediary and the
intermediated RP. IR 2025/848 Article 6(3-4) specifies that
registrars shall verify:
- (a) accuracy, validity, authenticity, and integrity of the Annex I
  information
- (b) where applicable, the power of attorney of RP representatives
- (c) the type of entitlement(s) of the RP (per Annex III)
- (d) absence of existing registration in another national register

Verification must use supporting documentation or authentic sources
(Art 6(4)). If verification fails, the Registrar SHALL reject the
registration (Art 6(6)).

This evidence requirement is critical for the wallet-side trust chain.
When a wallet user verifies an intermediary-RP relationship via the
Registrar (AS-RP-51-009, VEND-CORE-011), the Registrar's confirmation is
only as trustworthy as the evidence it originally verified.
requirements.legalText:
Where possible, registrars shall verify in an automated manner:
(a) the accuracy, validity, authenticity and integrity of the
information required under Article 5; (b) where applicable, the
power of attorney of representatives of the wallet-relying parties;
(c) the type of entitlement or entitlements of the wallet-relying
parties as set out in Annex I; (d) the absence of an existing
registration in another national register.

requirements.requirement: Perform verification of attestations as agreed with RP
requirements.explanation:
ARF HLR AS-RP-51-012 mandates that the intermediary SHALL verify attributes
presented by wallet units before forwarding them to the intermediated
RP (per the forward-only rule AS-RP-51-011). This is a critical trust
function — the intermediary acts as a verification gateway.

**Five verification dimensions (as specified in the ARF):**
1. **Authenticity**: verify the digital signature on the PID or
   attestation against the issuer's public key and trust chain
2. **Revocation status**: check that the PID/attestation has not been
   revoked (using Status Lists, OCSP, or equivalent mechanism per the
   attestation format)
3. **Device binding**: verify cryptographic proof that the credential
   is bound to the presenting wallet's secure element (WSCD)
4. **User binding**: verify proof that the authorised user is
   presenting the credential (biometric match, PIN verification, etc.)
5. **Wallet unit authenticity**: verify the Wallet Unit Attestation
   (WUA) and its revocation status

**The "as agreed" qualification (critical):**
The ARF explicitly notes that it does not mandate a Relying Party to
require all verifications. The intermediary and each RP must agree on
which verifications the intermediary will carry out. This creates a
per-RP configuration requirement — some RPs may require full
verification while others may accept partial checks.

**Conditional forwarding (AS-RP-51-011 interaction):**
If any of the agreed verifications fail, the intermediary SHALL NOT
forward any attributes to the RP. Successful verification is a
prerequisite for forwarding (VEND-CORE-001).

The eIDAS legal basis (Art 5b(9)) places ultimate responsibility for
verification on the RP, but the intermediary performs it as a delegate
per contractual agreement.
requirements.legalText:
Relying parties shall be responsible for carrying out the procedure 
for authenticating and validating person identification data and 
electronic attestation of attributes requested from European Digital 
Identity Wallets.

requirements.requirement: Implement TS12 for PSD2 Strong Customer Authentication when processing payment transactions
requirements.explanation:
Payment Service Providers (PSPs) using EUDI Wallets for Strong Customer
Authentication must implement ARF Technical Specification 12 (TS12),
which defines how the wallet's cryptographic binding, dynamic linking,
and attestation mechanisms satisfy PSD2 RTS requirements.

**PSD2 SCA requirements mapped to EUDI Wallet mechanisms:**
- **Two-factor authentication (Art 4)**: SCA requires at least two of
  three elements: knowledge (PIN/passphrase), possession (device/WSCD),
  inherence (biometric). The EUDI Wallet's user binding (biometric +
  device binding) natively satisfies possession and inherence.
- **Dynamic linking (Art 5)**: authentication must link the transaction
  to a specific amount and payee. The wallet can include transaction
  details in the signed presentation, creating a cryptographic binding.
- **Independence of elements (Art 9)**: compromise of one factor must
  not compromise others. The WSCD-backed key architecture provides
  hardware-level element separation.

**TS12 extends the standard OpenID4VP flow (TS5) to include:**
- Transaction metadata in presentation requests
- Signed acknowledgement of transaction details
- Integration points with PSP infrastructure (acquirer, card scheme)

This requirement is role-restricted: it applies only to vendors whose
products are used by PSPs for payment authentication. The vendor should
clarify which payment scenarios they support (in-store, online card-
not-present, account-to-account) and which SCA exemptions they handle
(low-value, recurring, trusted beneficiaries).
requirements.legalText:
Payment service providers shall apply strong customer authentication where 
the payer initiates an electronic payment transaction. The authentication 
shall include elements which dynamically link the transaction to a specific 
amount and a specific payee.

requirements.requirement: Implement TS6 (OpenID4VCI) for attestation issuance into EUDI Wallets
requirements.explanation:
Attestation Issuers must implement the OpenID for Verifiable Credential
Issuance (OpenID4VCI) protocol as specified in Technical Specification 6
(TS6). This ensures interoperability with all compliant EUDI Wallet
implementations across Member States.

**OpenID4VCI protocol flows:**
- **Pre-authorized code flow**: the issuer generates a credential offer
  (e.g., via QR code or deep link) containing a pre-authorized code.
  The wallet exchanges this for an access token and requests credential
  issuance. Used for scenarios where the user has already been
  authenticated outside the wallet (e.g., at a government counter).
- **Authorization code flow**: the wallet initiates issuance by
  directing the user to the issuer's authorization endpoint for
  authentication. After authorization, the wallet obtains an access
  token and requests credential issuance.
- **Deferred issuance**: the issuer returns a transaction ID indicating
  the credential is not yet ready. The wallet polls the deferred
  credential endpoint until issuance is complete.

**Key implementation requirements:**
- **Credential formats**: must support at least one of SD-JWT-VC
  (IETF-based) or mdoc (ISO 18013-5-based), as mandated by TS1
- **Wallet unit authentication**: the issuer must verify the WUA
  (Wallet Unit Attestation, per TS3) before binding credentials to
  the wallet's cryptographic keys (VEND-CORE-025)
- **Key binding**: issued credentials must be bound to the wallet
  unit's key pair within the WSCD
- **Same-device and cross-device**: support for both issuance models
  (same device via app-to-app, cross-device via QR code)

This requirement applies to issuance platforms and is restricted to
the issuer role.
requirements.legalText:
European Digital Identity Wallets shall use the protocols and interfaces 
set out in this Regulation for the issuance of person identification data 
and electronic attestations of attributes.

requirements.requirement: Implement TS7 data deletion interface and process requests within GDPR Article 17 timeframes
requirements.explanation:
Relying Parties must implement the common data deletion request interface
specified in Technical Specification 7 (TS7) and process deletion requests
in compliance with GDPR Article 17 timeframes. This enables wallet users
to exercise their right to erasure by requesting deletion of any data the
RP has collected from wallet presentations.

**The data deletion request chain (Topic 48):**
1. **User initiation (AS-WP-48-001-03)**: the wallet unit provides a
   function where the user can select an RP and initiate a deletion
   request via URL (web form), email (draft template), or phone call
2. **Registrar lookup (AS-RP-48-002)**: if no RP contact information
   is in the transaction log, the wallet unit queries the Registrar
   to obtain the RP's contact details
3. **Wallet logging (AS-WP-48-003-06)**: the wallet logs the deletion
   request initiation (date/time, RP identifier, attributes requested
   for deletion)
4. **RP authentication (AS-RP-48-005)**: before executing deletion, the
   RP SHALL authenticate the requesting user using appropriate
   mechanisms — the ARF recommends using the wallet's own
   authentication or signature facilities for this purpose
5. **RP compliance with TS7 (AS-WP-48-004)**: wallets, RPs, and
   Registrars must comply with the TS7 technical interface

**GDPR Article 17 processing requirements:**
- Deletion must be performed "without undue delay" and in any event
  within one month (Art 12(3))
- The RP must inform the user of any valid grounds for refusal under
  Art 17(3) exceptions: freedom of expression, legal obligation,
  public interest, health, archiving/research, legal claims
- If the data has been made public, the RP must take reasonable
  steps to inform other controllers processing the data (Art 17(2))
- All copies including backups must be addressed (though backup
  deletion may follow a deferred schedule)

**Key obligations for the RP connector:**
- Implement the TS7 standardised interface for receiving deletion
  requests in a machine-readable format
- Authenticate the requesting user before executing deletion
- Provide confirmation of deletion or a reasoned refusal following
  the TS7 standardised response format
- Handle Art 17(3) exceptions where deletion may be refused

In the EUDI Wallet connector context, the connector may receive
deletion requests for data it processed on behalf of the RP. Given
the no-storage mandate (VEND-CORE-001), the connector's deletable
data is limited to transaction metadata and audit logs — but the
interface must still be implemented. This requirement connects to
VEND-CORE-029 (EW-DM-44-012 deletion contact information in registration
certificates).
requirements.legalText:
The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller the 
erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay and 
the controller shall have the obligation to erase personal data without 
undue delay.

requirements.requirement: Register attestation schemas in the catalogue per TS11
requirements.explanation:
Attestation Issuers must register their attestation types in the EU
catalogue of attributes and attestations as specified in Technical
Specification 11 (TS11). This catalogue is the authoritative registry
enabling discovery and interoperability across the EUDI Wallet ecosystem.

**Catalogue structure and governance:**
- The catalogue defines the **common data model** for attestation
  schemas — a standardised way to describe attribute names, types,
  encodings, and validity rules
- **Rulebooks** govern sector-specific attestation structures (e.g.,
  mobile driving licence per ISO 18013-5, payment credentials, health
  records). Issuers must follow the relevant rulebook for their
  attestation type
- The catalogue maps the relationship between attestation types and
  the attributes they contain, enabling RPs and wallets to discover
  what attributes are available for specific attestation types

**Registration obligations:**
- Qualified trust service providers issuing QEAAs must ensure their
  schemas comply with the TS11 specifications (IR 2024/2981 Art 3(1))
- Schemas must be registered before attestation issuance begins
- Schema versioning must be managed — updates to schemas must be
  registered and backward compatibility considered

**Interoperability impact:**
Catalogue registration ensures that a verifier (RP or intermediary) in
any Member State can validate the structure and encoding of attestations
issued by any compliant issuer. Without catalogue registration, cross-
border interoperability of attestations is not possible.

This requirement applies to issuance platforms and is restricted to
the issuer role.
requirements.legalText:
Qualified trust service providers issuing qualified electronic attestations 
of attributes shall ensure that the attestation schemas they use comply 
with the technical specifications set out in this Regulation.

requirements.requirement: Implement open standards per TS1 for EUDI Wallet interoperability
requirements.explanation:
All EUDI Wallet ecosystem participants must implement the open standards
mapped in Technical Specification 1 (TS1). TS1 is the authoritative
standards index — it provides the definitive mapping between regulatory
requirements and the specific open standards that must be used.

**Core standards mapped by TS1:**
- **OpenID4VCI**: issuance protocol (TS6, VEND-CORE-020)
- **OpenID4VP**: presentation/verification protocol (TS5)
- **SD-JWT-VC**: IETF-based credential format for selective disclosure
- **mdoc/mDL (ISO 18013-5)**: ISO-based credential format for mobile
  documents
- **ISO 23220**: extended mobile document specifications
- **Status Lists**: credential revocation checking

**Format duality (SD-JWT + mdoc):**
The EUDI Wallet ecosystem mandates support for two credential format
families:
1. **SD-JWT-VC**: JSON-based, using selective disclosure JWT mechanism.
   Supports selective disclosure at the claim level.
2. **mdoc**: CBOR-based, derived from mobile driving licence standard.
   Uses CBOR encoding with MSO (Mobile Security Object) for integrity.

Intermediaries and connectors must be able to verify both formats.
Issuance platforms typically specialise in one format based on the
attestation type (e.g., mDL uses mdoc, PIDs may use either).

**Interoperability testing:**
Vendors should demonstrate interoperability through participation in
EU-organised plugfest events, cross-vendor testing, and conformance
test suites. The evolving nature of draft specifications (particularly
OpenID4VCI and OpenID4VP drafts) requires active standards tracking
and version management.

**Vendor lock-in prevention:**
Article 5a(23) eIDAS requires open standards specifically to prevent
vendor lock-in. Any proprietary extensions beyond the TS1-mapped
standards should be clearly documented and justified.
requirements.legalText:
The protocols and interfaces for European Digital Identity Wallets shall 
be based on open standards to ensure interoperability across Member States.

requirements.requirement: Publish provider information per TS2 for discovery by wallets and RPs
requirements.explanation:
PID Providers, QEAA Providers, and Pub-EAA Providers must publish their
provider information according to Technical Specification 2 (TS2). This
publication enables the discovery layer of the EUDI Wallet ecosystem —
wallets and RPs can dynamically discover available attestation providers
and their capabilities.

**Published metadata must include:**
- **Issuer identifier**: unique identifier for the provider within the
  EUDI Wallet trust framework
- **Supported credential types**: which attestation types the provider
  can issue (PID, QEAA, Pub-EAA), linked to catalogue entries (TS11,
  VEND-CORE-022)
- **Credential formats**: which formats are supported for each type
  (SD-JWT-VC, mdoc, or both per TS1)
- **Signing algorithms**: cryptographic algorithms used for credential
  signing (aligned with TS1 algorithm profile)
- **Trust chain information**: how the provider's signing keys chain
  to the EUDI Wallet trust anchors
- **Endpoints**: credential, authorization, and token endpoints per
  the OpenID4VCI protocol (TS6, VEND-CORE-020)

**Publication requirements:**
- Metadata must be published in machine-readable format at a
  well-known URL (per OpenID4VCI issuer metadata specification)
- Updates must be reflected promptly when service configuration changes
  (e.g., new credential types, algorithm rotations)
- High availability is expected — wallet and RP discovery flows depend
  on metadata endpoint accessibility

This requirement applies to issuance platforms and is restricted to
the issuer role. For intermediaries acting as connectors, the
requirement applies to the extent they need to discover and relay
provider information to intermediated RPs.
requirements.legalText:
Providers of qualified electronic attestations of attributes shall notify 
their activities to the supervisory body and publish information about 
their services in a machine-readable format.

requirements.requirement: Verify Wallet Unit Attestation (WUA) per TS3 before issuing credentials
requirements.explanation:
Before issuing attestations to a wallet unit, issuers must verify the
Wallet Unit Attestation (WUA) as specified in Technical Specification 3
(TS3). The WUA is the cornerstone of the EUDI Wallet trust model —
it cryptographically proves that the target wallet instance is
legitimate and trustworthy.

**WUA verification checks:**
1. **Signature validation**: verify the WUA's digital signature against
   the Wallet Provider's signing key
2. **Certificate chain**: validate the chain from the WUA signing key
   to the trust anchor in the EUDI Wallet Trusted List
3. **Revocation status**: check that the WUA has not been revoked
   (indicating a compromised or decommissioned wallet unit)
4. **WSCD certification**: verify that the wallet's secure cryptographic
   device (WSCD) is certified — this confirms the hardware security
   level of key storage
5. **Key possession proof**: verify that the wallet unit holds the
   private key corresponding to the key pair in the WUA

**Security rationale:**
Without WUA verification, an issuer could bind credentials to:
- A compromised wallet unit (keys extracted)
- A non-certified wallet (inadequate key protection)
- A revoked wallet (no longer under user's sole control)

**Issuance flow integration:**
WUA verification occurs during the OpenID4VCI credential request
(TS6, VEND-CORE-020). The wallet presents its WUA alongside the
proof-of-possession for the key pair. If WUA verification fails,
the issuer SHALL reject the credential request and return an
appropriate error response.

This requirement applies to issuance platforms and trust services.
requirements.legalText:
Before issuing person identification data or electronic attestations of 
attributes, providers shall verify the authenticity and validity of the 
European Digital Identity Wallet to which the credential is to be issued.

requirements.requirement: Implement TS8 remote signing protocol for QES/QESeal via EUDI Wallet
requirements.explanation:
Trust service providers offering remote qualified electronic signatures
(QES) or qualified electronic seals (QESeal) must implement the protocol
specified in Technical Specification 8 (TS8). This enables EUDI Wallet
users to create legally binding electronic signatures using QTSP-managed
signing keys while maintaining sole control through wallet-based
authorisation.

**Remote signing architecture:**
- **Server Signing Application (SSA)**: the QTSP's server-side component
  that manages signing keys in a Qualified Signature Creation Device
  (QSCD — typically an HSM)
- **Wallet-based authorisation**: the user authorises each signing
  operation through the EUDI Wallet, which acts as the Sole Control
  Interface (SCI). Multi-factor authentication is required for each
  signing operation
- **WYSIWYS**: What You See Is What You Sign — the user must be shown
  the document to be signed before authorising. The wallet or the
  signing application must render the document faithfully

**Key security requirements:**
- Signing keys must be generated and stored exclusively in certified
  QSCDs (Art 29(1) eIDAS for QES)
- The user must have sole control over the signing key activation
  (Art 26(1)(c) eIDAS)
- Each signing operation must be independently authorised — batch
  signing requires per-document or per-batch explicit consent
- The link between the signing key and the user's identity must be
  established through the PID in the wallet

**Document format support:**
The signing protocol must support at least PAdES (PDF), XAdES (XML),
CAdES (binary), and JAdES (JSON) signature formats to cover the
range of eIDAS-mandated signature types.

This requirement applies to trust service providers and is role-
restricted to the issuer (QTSP) role.
requirements.legalText:
An advanced electronic signature shall meet the requirements of being 
uniquely linked to and capable of identifying the signatory, created 
using electronic signature creation data that the signatory can use 
under their sole control.

requirements.requirement: Support pseudonym attestations per TS9 for privacy-preserving identification
requirements.explanation:
RPs and Issuers must support pseudonym attestations as specified in
Technical Specification 9 (TS9) when full identification is not legally
required. Article 5a(4)(b) eIDAS mandates that EUDI Wallets enable
selective disclosure "including by means of pseudonyms", and Art 5b(9)
prohibits RPs from refusing pseudonyms where identification is not
required by law.

**Pseudonym types (per ARF Topic 11):**
- **User Pseudonyms (UP)**: persistent pseudonymous identifiers that
  allow a user to maintain an ongoing relationship with an RP without
  revealing their true identity. Useful for subscription services,
  loyalty programs, or recurring interactions
- **Wallet-RP Pseudonyms (WRP)**: per-RP, per-session pseudonyms that
  prevent cross-RP linkability. Each interaction generates a fresh
  pseudonym, ensuring that two RPs cannot collude to correlate users

**Privacy preservation mechanisms:**
- **Selective disclosure**: present only the minimum attributes required
  (e.g., "age over 18" instead of full date of birth)
- **Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP)**: prove a property about an attribute
  without revealing the attribute value itself
- **Unlinkability**: ensure that multiple presentations by the same user
  to different RPs (or even the same RP at different times) cannot be
  correlated

**Re-identification safeguards:**
Pseudonymous users may need to be re-identified in specific circumstances
(court order, fraud investigation). The mechanism for re-identification
must be legally grounded and procedurally constrained.

For the intermediary context, the intermediary must preserve the
pseudonymous nature of the presentation when forwarding attributes —
it must not de-pseudonymise or add correlatable metadata.
requirements.legalText:
European Digital Identity Wallets shall enable the user to selectively 
disclose to relying parties person identification data, electronic 
attestation of attributes, or specific data elements of such data or 
attestations, including by means of pseudonyms.

requirements.requirement: Provide data export capability per TS10 for GDPR portability compliance
requirements.explanation:
RPs and Issuers must provide data export capabilities as specified in
Technical Specification 10 (TS10). This supports GDPR Article 20 data
portability rights, enabling users to obtain and transfer their data
in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format.

**Data portability scope in the EUDI Wallet context:**
- **Transaction logs**: history of attestation presentations, issuances,
  and data deletion requests
- **User preferences**: stored consent records, selective disclosure
  configurations, and RP relationship metadata
- **Credential backup data**: depending on the wallet architecture,
  users may need to export credential metadata for migration between
  wallet providers

**GDPR Art 20 requirements:**
- Data must be provided in a structured, commonly used, and machine-
  readable format (Art 20(1))
- Where technically feasible, the user has the right to have data
  transmitted directly from one controller to another (Art 20(2))
- The right applies only to data "provided by" the data subject and
  processed on consent or contract basis

**Implementation obligations:**
- Self-service export interface to minimise processing time
- Support for at least one structured/machine-readable format
  (JSON recommended, XML and CSV as alternatives)
- Secure transmission of exported data (encryption in transit and
  at rest during download)
- Response within the Art 12(3) one-month deadline

For intermediaries, the portability scope is limited to the data the
intermediary holds as processor — primarily transaction metadata and
audit logs, given the no-storage mandate (VEND-CORE-001).
requirements.legalText:
The data subject shall have the right to receive the personal data 
concerning him or her, which he or she has provided to a controller, 
in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and have 
the right to transmit those data to another controller.

requirements.requirement: Verify registration certificates presented by counterparties
requirements.explanation:
Relying Parties must verify registration certificates presented by PID
Providers, Attestation Providers, or other RPs (Topic 44). Registration
certificates are the EUDI Wallet ecosystem's mechanism for conveying
verified registration information in cryptographically signed form.

**Registration certificate verification chain (RPRC HLRs):**
- **EW-DM-44-003**: certificate contents must include at least the
  information required in Annex V of IR 2025/848
- **EW-DM-44-006**: if the subject is not an RP (i.e., a provider), the
  certificate SHALL NOT contain intended use (Annex I pts 9-10)
- **EW-DM-44-011**: if an RP received registration certificates during
  registration, it SHALL distribute these to all its RP Instances
- **EW-DM-44-012**: the certificate SHALL contain at least one data deletion
  contact channel (web form URL, email, or phone number)
- **EW-DM-44-013**: the certificate SHALL contain the supervising DPA's
  name, country, and contact information for reporting suspicious
  attribute requests

**Verification steps:**
1. Validate the certificate's digital signature
2. Verify the certificate chain to a trusted anchor
3. Check the certificate's revocation status
4. Validate the certificate contents against the expected structure
5. Verify the intended use matches the actual data request

Art 5b(7) provides the legal basis: Member States must provide a
"common mechanism for allowing the identification and authentication
of relying parties". Registration certificates are the realisation
of this mechanism.
requirements.legalText:
Member States shall provide a common mechanism for allowing the 
identification and authentication of relying parties, as referred 
to in Article 5a(5), point (c).

requirements.requirement: Verify attestation authenticity and validity before acceptance
requirements.explanation:
Before accepting any attestation (PID, QEAA, Pub-EAA, or non-qualified
EAA), the RP must perform a multi-step verification process. This
implements Art 5b(9) eIDAS, which places verification responsibility
squarely on the RP.

**Verification requirements per attestation type (EW-PIO-01-020-15):**
- **PID**: validate signature using the trust anchor from the national
  Trusted List (EW-PIO-01-020)
- **QEAA**: validate signature using the trust anchor from the QEAA
  Trusted List (EW-PIO-01-021)
- **Pub-EAA**: validate signature using the trust anchor provided by
  the Member State (EW-PIO-01-022)
- **Non-qualified EAA**: validate signature using the trust anchor
  specified in the applicable Rulebook (EW-PIO-01-023) — additional issuer
  authorisation verification may be required

**Unique element handling (AS-RP-01-002 — critical privacy requirement):**
After verification, the RP SHALL discard the values of all unique
elements (AS-AP-10-056 elements + timestamps) as soon as they are no longer
needed. These values SHALL NOT be communicated to the RP backend or
any other party. This prevents correlation and tracking.

**Additional verification steps:**
- Check attestation expiry (validity period)
- Verify revocation status (Status Lists, OCSP)
- Verify the issuer's access certificate chain
- For intermediaries: perform verification before forwarding
  (VEND-CORE-018, AS-RP-51-012)

The RP must distinguish between attestation types at verification
time because each type has a different trust anchor source. This
requires the RP to maintain and regularly update multiple trust
anchor stores.
requirements.legalText:
Relying parties shall be responsible for carrying out the procedure 
for authenticating and validating person identification data and 
electronic attestation of attributes requested from European Digital 
Identity Wallets.

requirements.requirement: Register intended uses and comply with access certificate policies
requirements.explanation:
Relying Parties must register their intended uses and comply with the
access certificate policies established by Access Certificate Authorities
(ACAs). This is the mechanism that enforces data minimisation at the
ecosystem level — an RP can only request data elements that match its
registered intended uses.

**Intended use registration (Art 5b(2)(c)):**
- An RP must specify which categories of data it intends to request
  from wallet users
- This registration is validated by the Registrar and encoded into
  the RP's access certificate (AS-MS-27-038: user-friendly name; AS-MS-27-039:
  EU-wide unique identifier)
- The wallet uses the intended use in the access certificate to
  verify that the RP's actual data request matches its registration

**Access certificate policy compliance (AS-MS-27-018):**
The common Certificate Policy SHALL include a revocation policy
requiring ACA revocation when:
- The RP is suspended or cancelled by its Registrar
- On request of the certificate subject (the RP)
- On request of a competent national authority

**Intended use enforcement chain:**
1. RP registers intended uses → Registrar validates
2. ACA issues access certificate containing intended uses
3. RP includes access certificate in presentation requests (formerly AS-RP-06-001)
4. Wallet verifies intended use matches actual request
5. If mismatch → wallet can warn user or block presentation

For intermediaries, intended use registration must cover the
intended uses of each intermediated RP (per AS-RP-51-003, VEND-CORE-016).
The intermediary's own access certificate and the intermediated RP's
registration certificate must be consistent.
requirements.legalText:
Relying parties shall not request users to provide any data other 
than that indicated pursuant to paragraph 2, point (c).

requirements.requirement: Use valid RP Access Certificate for Wallet Unit authentication
requirements.explanation:
When initiating a presentation request, the Relying Party must present
a valid RP Access Certificate that allows the Wallet Unit to verify
the RP's registration and intended use. This is the mechanism that
gives the wallet user confidence that the RP is legitimate and has
only registered to request the specific data elements it is asking for.

**Access certificate inclusion (formerly AS-RP-06-001, emptied in ARF v2.8.0):**
The RP Instance SHALL include its access certificates in the
presentation request **by value, not by reference**. This design
decision ensures:
- No external requests are necessary to carry out RP authentication
- Transactions are atomic and self-contained
- Offline/proximity scenarios work without internet connectivity

**Wallet-side verification (AS-WP-06-007):**
If RP authentication succeeds, the Wallet Instance SHALL display to
the User:
- The name of the Relying Party as included in the access certificate
- The attributes requested by the Relying Party
- For intermediary RPs: the names of both the intermediary and the
  intermediated RP (per AS-RP-51-008)

**Authentication failure handling (AS-WP-06-008):**
If RP authentication fails for any reason, the Wallet Unit SHALL
notify the User and SHALL either:
- Not present any attributes to the RP, or
- Give the User the choice to present or not

**Certificate contents:**
The access certificate encodes the RP's identity, the intended use
(per VEND-CORE-031), and the signing chain to a notified ACA trust
anchor. The wallet validates the certificate chain, checks revocation
status, and verifies the intended use matches the actual request.

Art 5b(8) requires RPs to identify themselves to the user when
relying on EUDI Wallets — the access certificate is the technical
instrument that fulfils this obligation.
requirements.legalText:
Where relying parties intend to rely upon European Digital Identity 
Wallets, they shall identify themselves to the user.

requirements.requirement: Support and correctly handle pseudonym-based presentations
requirements.explanation:
Where Users choose to present pseudonymous attestations, the RP
connector must correctly process these presentations without
attempting to de-pseudonymise the user. Article 5a(16) requires the
EUDI Wallet technical framework to prevent tracking and correlation,
and Art 5b(9) explicitly prohibits RPs from refusing pseudonyms where
identification is not legally required.

**Pseudonym verification requirements (PA HLRs):**
- **AS-WP-11-011**: the RP SHALL be able to verify that the User is
  registering a Pseudonym using a **non-revoked** Wallet Unit
- **AS-WP-11-012**: the RP SHALL be able to verify that the User is
  authenticating with a Pseudonym using a **non-revoked** Wallet Unit
- **AS-WP-11-014**: the RP SHALL be able to validate that the pseudonym
  presented belongs to the User presenting it (binding verification)

**Privacy safeguards (critical):**
- **AS-WP-11-016**: the RP SHALL NOT be able to derive the User's true
  identity, or any data identifying the User, from the Pseudonym
  value received
- **AS-WP-11-018**: it SHALL NOT be possible to correlate Pseudonyms based
  on their values or other metadata sent by the Wallet Unit during
  registration and authentication — colluding RPs SHALL NOT be able
  to conclude that different Pseudonyms belong to the same User

**Implementation obligations for RP connector:**
- Accept pseudonym attestations in the same flow as identified
  attestations (no separate code path that could leak identity)
- Strip or avoid logging any metadata that could enable correlation
  (IP addresses, session IDs, timing patterns)
- Do not transmit pseudonym values to backend systems that also
  process identified presentations for the same service
- Where the RP legitimately needs re-identification (Art 5b(9)
  exception), use a legally grounded procedure with independent
  oversight

This requirement complements VEND-CORE-027 (TS9 pseudonym support)
by focusing on the RP-side processing obligations rather than the
issuance/wallet-side mechanisms.

**Rate-limited pseudonyms (ARF v2.8.0, AS-WP-11-026/AS-WP-11-027):**
v2.8.0 introduces scope rate-limited pseudonyms (AS-WP-11-024–AS-WP-11-032).
When these are deployed, RPs will need to:
- **AS-WP-11-026**: verify that a user's pseudonym rate is not exceeded
- **AS-WP-11-027**: specify the scope and rate when requesting a
  rate-limited pseudonym from a user
These HLRs are not yet referenced as mandatory because the
underlying protocol is still being specified, but RP vendors
should plan for this capability.
requirements.legalText:
The technical framework of the European Digital Identity Wallet shall 
not allow providers of electronic attestations of attributes or any 
other party, after the issuance of the attestation of attributes, to 
obtain data that allows transactions or user behaviour to be tracked, 
linked or correlated, or knowledge of transactions or user behaviour 
to be otherwise obtained, unless explicitly authorised by the user.

requirements.requirement: Publish RP trust anchor information for Wallet verification
requirements.explanation:
Relying Parties accessing EUDI Wallets must ensure their access
certificates and registration certificates can be authenticated
using the trust anchors of a notified Access Certificate Authority
(ACA) or Provider of registration certificates. This is the RP-side
obligation that complements the wallet's verification chain.

**ACA notification requirements (RPACANot HLRs):**
- **AS-MS-31-015**: RPs, PID Providers, QEAA Providers, Pub-EAA
  Providers, and non-qualified EAA Providers SHALL ensure that their
  **access certificates** can be authenticated using the trust
  anchors of an ACA **notified to the Commission**
- **AS-MS-31-016**: the same parties SHALL ensure that their
  **registration certificates**, if issued to them, can be
  authenticated using the trust anchors of a **Provider of
  registration certificates notified to the Commission**

**Publication and discoverability:**
Art 5b(5) requires Member States to make RP registration information
publicly available online in electronically signed or sealed form
suitable for automated processing. This means:
- RP trust anchor information must be discoverable by wallets and
  other ecosystem participants
- The publication format must support automated machine processing
- Electronic signatures/seals on the published information must be
  verifiable

**Operational implications:**
- The RP must select and onboard with a notified ACA before operating
- If the chosen ACA loses its notification status, the RP must
  migrate to another notified ACA
- Trust anchor updates (key rotations) must be coordinated with the
  ACA to avoid disruption

This requirement is foundational for the EUDI Wallet trust model:
if wallet units cannot verify RP access certificates, they cannot
authenticate RPs, and the entire presentation flow breaks down.
requirements.legalText:
Member States shall make the information referred to in paragraph 2 
publicly available online in electronically signed or sealed form 
suitable for automated processing.

requirements.requirement: Support W3C Digital Credentials API for presentation requests
requirements.explanation:
If the Relying Party supports browser-based wallet interactions, it
must conform to the W3C Digital Credentials API specification. This
API provides the standardised browser-mediated credential exchange
flow that enables wallet attestations to be presented through web
browsers.

**API processing constraints (EW-PIO-01-014 — strict privacy rule):**
If a Relying Party supports the W3C Digital Credentials API, the
presentation request:
- **MAY** be processed by the browser/OS for: searching available
  attestations, preventing fraud targeting the User, or
  troubleshooting purposes
- **SHOULD** be processed by the browser/OS for: User security
  purposes
- **SHALL NOT** be processed by the browser/OS for: market analysis
  purposes (including as a secondary purpose) or for the browser's/
  OS's own purposes

This "SHALL NOT for market analysis" constraint is critical — it
prevents browser vendors from using attestation request data to
build user profiles or sell advertising insights.

**Implementation considerations:**
- The API flow differs from the OpenID4VP same-device flow and
  requires specific browser integration
- Browser support is evolving; the RP must handle fallback for
  browsers that do not yet support the API
- The W3C Digital Credentials API provides a more user-friendly
  experience than deep-link or QR-code based flows for desktop
  browsers
- Cross-origin security protections apply — the RP must properly
  configure CORS and Content-Security-Policy headers

**Relationship to OpenID4VP:**
The W3C Digital Credentials API can serve as the transport layer
for OpenID4VP requests in same-device web browser scenarios,
while OpenID4VP handles cross-device flows via QR codes.
requirements.legalText:
Where relying parties intend to rely upon European Digital Identity 
Wallets, they shall identify themselves to the user.

requirements.requirement: Handle revocation status unavailability gracefully
requirements.explanation:
When revocation status information is temporarily unavailable, the
Relying Party Instance must implement intelligent fallback behaviour
rather than repeatedly hammering the status endpoint. AS-AP-07-022
specifies a privacy-preserving approach to revocation checking that
prevents correlation.

**Privacy-preserving revocation checking (AS-AP-07-022):**
- The RP Instance SHOULD NOT request the relevant Attestation Status
  List or Attestation Revocation List each time an attestation is
  presented by a Wallet Unit
- Instead, the Relying Party operating the RP Instance SHOULD
  download each new version of the list **once**, at a time and from
  a location **unrelated to the presentation** of a PID or
  attestation by a User
- The RP SHOULD then distribute the list to all of its RP Instances
  using an RP-internal distribution mechanism

**Rationale (privacy-critical):**
If the RP fetches revocation status at the time of presentation,
the status provider (typically the issuer) can correlate:
- Which RP is checking which attestation
- When the attestation was presented
- Potentially, which user presented it

By pre-fetching and internally distributing status lists, this
correlation vector is eliminated.

**Unavailability handling:**
When the status list endpoint is unreachable:
1. Use the most recent cached version of the status list
2. Implement exponential backoff for retry attempts
3. Alert operations teams if unavailability exceeds a threshold
4. Decide on a fail-open vs fail-closed policy based on the
   risk profile of the service (high-assurance services should
   fail closed; low-risk services may accept cached status)

For intermediary deployments, the intermediary should maintain
its own status list cache and not rely on per-presentation
fetches, aligning with the same privacy rationale.
requirements.legalText:
Relying parties shall be responsible for carrying out the procedure 
for authenticating and validating person identification data and 
electronic attestation of attributes requested from European Digital 
Identity Wallets.

requirements.requirement: Support proximity identification flows (optional)
requirements.explanation:
Relying Party Instances may optionally support proximity
identification flows for face-to-face scenarios where the user
presents their wallet physically (e.g., border control, age
verification at point-of-sale, in-branch identity verification).

**Protocol requirements (EW-PIO-24-002):**
If an RP supports proximity flows, its RP Instances SHALL support
**device retrieval** as specified in ISO/IEC 18013-5 for requesting
PID or attestation attributes. Such RP Instances SHALL comply with
the requirements for **mDL readers and mdoc readers** in
ISO/IEC 18013-5. This means:
- BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) as the mandatory transport
- NFC as an optional transport
- Device engagement via QR code or NFC tap
- Secure session establishment with ephemeral key agreement

**Offline operation:**
Proximity flows are specifically designed for scenarios without
internet connectivity. The RP Instance performs all verification
locally using pre-loaded trust anchors and cached revocation
status. This imposes requirements on the RP Instance:
- Pre-load all necessary issuer trust anchors
- Cache revocation status lists locally (connects to VEND-CORE-039)
- Perform all cryptographic verification on-device

**Security considerations:**
ISO/IEC 18013-5 specifies HKDF-based key derivation, AES-256-GCM
encryption, and device authentication via ECDSA signatures. The
RP's reader device must support these cryptographic operations.

**Note:** Support for proximity flows is NOT mandatory per the ARF.
This is a MAY requirement. However, if implemented, conformance
to ISO/IEC 18013-5 is mandatory.
requirements.legalText:
The European Digital Identity Wallet shall, in particular, enable 
the user to electronically identify and authenticate online and 
offline, in both cross-border and domestic scenarios, for the purpose 
of accessing public and private services.

requirements.requirement: Handle registration certificate updates and renewals
requirements.explanation:
Relying Parties must properly handle the full lifecycle of their
registration certificates, including updates, renewals, and
revocations. Registration certificates are the EUDI Wallet
ecosystem's mechanism for conveying verified RP information
(identity, intended use, registered attributes) in cryptographically
signed form.

**Include by value (EW-DM-44-017):**
If an RP Instance received one or more registration certificates
(via EW-DM-44-011), it SHALL include **a single registration certificate
applicable for its current intended use** in each presentation
request to a Wallet Unit. The certificate SHALL be included **by
value, not by reference**. This applies to both proximity and remote
flows.

**EW-DM-44-018 extension fields:**
The RP Instance SHALL include in each presentation request:
a) the user-friendly name of the RP
b) the unique identifier of the RP
c) a user-friendly description of the intended use
d) the URL of the Registrar of the RP
e) the identifier of the intended use

These fields enable wallet-side verification: the wallet can use
items (c) and (d) to query the Registrar and verify that the
requested attributes match the RP's registration (EW-DM-44-021).

**Lifecycle events to handle:**
- **Renewal before expiry**: proactive replacement of certificates
  approaching expiration (monitor notBefore/notAfter)
- **Content update**: when registration details change (e.g., new
  intended use, changed RP name, updated privacy policy URL)
- **Revocation**: immediate removal and replacement when a
  certificate is compromised or the registration is suspended
- **Key rotation**: coordinated update when the signing key or
  trust anchor of the Provider of registration certificates changes
- **Distribution**: updated certificates must be propagated to all
  RP Instances (per EW-DM-44-011)

**Failure impact:**
If the RP presents an expired or revoked registration certificate,
the wallet will notify the user (EW-DM-44-016 fallback) and the user
may decline the transaction. This directly impacts conversion rates.
requirements.legalText:
Member States shall ensure that relying parties register the 
intended use of the European Digital Identity Wallets.

requirements.requirement: Apply personal data safeguards by default to all attestation processing
requirements.explanation:
Vendor products must apply GDPR Article 28 (processor obligations) and 
Article 32 (security of processing) safeguards by default to ALL attestation 
processing, regardless of whether specific attestation content appears to be 
personal data.

While eIDAS 2.0 Article 3(43) defines "attribute" as covering natural persons, 
legal persons, AND objects, the processing environment almost always contains 
personal data context (session tokens, wallet identifiers, IP addresses). 
Therefore, the product architecture must assume personal data processing.

This "Compliance by Environment" principle means:
- Default to GDPR-compliant data handling for all attestations
- Apply encryption, access controls, and audit logging universally
- Do not create separate "non-personal data" processing paths that bypass 
  security controls
- Treat the combination of attestation + session context as personal data

The customer (RP) may document exceptions for truly anonymous processing 
scenarios, but the product must not assume such exceptions.
requirements.legalText:
'personal data' means any information relating to an identified or 
identifiable natural person ('data subject'); an identifiable natural 
person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular 
by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, 
location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific 
to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or 
social identity of that natural person.
requirements.notes:
This requirement implements the "Compliance by Environment" principle 
established in DEC-281 (Jan 2026 Alignment Audit). Even if a specific 
attestation relates to an object or organization (not personal data per se), 
the wallet session context and processing metadata create an identifiable 
data subject context.

Exceptions (attestations that may not require full GDPR safeguards):
- Pure boolean ZKP proofs with high unlinkability
- Device-only attestations with no wallet user context
- Anonymous aggregate attestations

However, the PRODUCT should not make these determinations - the CUSTOMER 
(RP as data controller) documents exceptions in their DPIA.
